title: Beyond the Lesson Plan: The Four Moves of Effective Lesson Preparation reparation/
author: Sadie McCleary
source: Teach Like a Champion Blog (teachlikeachampion.org), November 4, 2026
summary: Sadie McCleary of Teach Like a Champion separates a lesson plan, which says what content will be taught, from lesson preparation, which is the set of decisions about how to teach it. She names four practices: planning the exemplar, planning for error with Back Pocket Questions, planning for active observation, and planning the means of participation as a full sequence. To make them concrete she walks through a second-grade ELA sample from Danielle Dahl at Desert Willow Elementary in Carlsbad, New Mexico. Dahl underlined and numbered text evidence in her exemplars, circled the word because as a point of difficulty, and planned observation laps while circulating. Her collected data showed which students had the evidence but not the connection, which shaped how she reviewed the question and whose paper to show. McCleary also highlights a subtle move, Standardize the Format, in which the teacher writes preparation directly on the same handout students use so attention is not split.
points: Lesson preparation is distinguished from lesson planning as the decisions about how to teach the plan, and it consists of four practices.
Drafting the exemplar response, including key vocabulary and evidence, gives the teacher a standard to compare student work against.
Anticipating errors and marking points of difficulty lets the teacher pay extra attention where students are likely to slip.
Planned observation laps while circulating produce data that decides how to review the question and whose work to Show Call.
Writing preparation on the same handout students use, called Standardize the Format, lets the teacher compare without splitting attention.
quotes: Lesson Preparation is a different process that involves making a series of decisions about how to teach that lesson plan. Strong preparation creates a strong student learning experience and enables more effective and flexible instruction
Planning the Exemplar: Drafting the ideal response, including vocabulary and key ideas, you’d expect your students to produce for core tasks and questions.
Planning for Error: Anticipating and planning responses to gaps/errors that may appear in student responses to core tasks and questions.

In her preparation, she first underlined the key evidence for each question within the text and numbered it as part of her exemplar planning. This will support her in Actively Observing for annotations and allow her to efficiently prompt students to return to the text if they haven’t yet cited evidence.
She has also circled ‘because’ as a key word in her exemplars and labeled it as a potential error (she uses the abbreviation “POD” or Point of Difficulty).

While Kaida and Kimber had superb answers, a handful of students had correct text evidence but didn’t make a strong connection. Based on this data, she could make an informed decision about how to review question 1 and whose paper to Show Call.

Danielle has written her prep directly onto the same handout that students use in class. We call this Standardize the Format. It means that Danielle can easily look between her own preparation in hand and what students are writing without having to split her attention.
